## Methods

Protein expression and purification
As previously reported23, we constructed human FOXO3a (residues 1-284), the NTD (residues 1-146) and the CTD (residues 141-284) and purified them. In addition, the mutants FOXO3a (T32A) and FOXO3a (S253A) were generated according to the QuikChange® mutagenesis protocol (Stratagene, La Jolla, CA, USA) using the pGEX-6P-1-FOXO3a plasmid as the template and were purified in the same way as the FOXO3a purification. FOXO3a, FOXO3a (T32A), NTD, and CTD were phosphorylated by AKT23 and FOXO3a (S253A) required the addition of three times the amount of AKT for the phosphorylation. The phosphorylation reaction proceeded completely, confirmed by MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry, using MALDI-8020 spectrometer (SHIMADZU). In the MALDI-TOF MS, α-cyano-4-hydroxycinnamic acid was used as the matrix for FOXO3a, FOXO3a (T32A), FOXO3a (S253A), and the NTD, and sinapinic acid was used for the measurement with CTD. These experiments were performed in a buffer containing 50% acetonitrile and 0.1% TFA. pNTD was additionally purified by reversed-phase chromatography.

The DNA sequence encoding full-length human 14-3-3ζ (residues 1-245), D197A/E198A/E202A/D204A mutant, and T215A/L216A/Q219A/R222A mutant were cloned into the pGEX-6P-1 (Cytiva). The glutathione-S-transferase-fusion proteins were expressed in Escherichia coli C41 (DE3) cells and induced by addition of isopropyl β-D-thiogalactopyranoside at a final concentration of 1 mM for 4 h at 37 °C. The cells were collected by centrifugation and disrupted by sonication in a buffer containing phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) (pH 7.4), 1 M NaCl, 10% glycerol, 1 mM phenylmethanesulfonyl fluoride, 1 mM DTT, and 0.1% polyethylenimine. Cell debris was removed by centrifugation, and the supernatant was purified using a Glutathione-SepharoseTM 4B column (Cytiva) in a buffer containing PBS (pH 7.4), 500 mM NaCl, 1 mM DTT and 10 mM reduced glutathione. Followed by digestion with PreScission Protease (Cytiva), the cleaved glutathione-S-transferase and noncleaved fusion proteins were removed using a Glutathione-SepharoseTM 4B column. The impurities were removed using an anion exchange column (CaptoTM HiRes Q 5/50 GL; Cytiva) in a linear gradient of 0–1 M NaCl in 20 mM Tris-HCl (pH 7.5) and 1 mM DTT. 14-3-3ζ mutants were additionally purified by gel filtration using SuperdexTM 200 increase 10/300 GL (Cytiva) in a buffer containing 20 mM NaPi (pH 7.4), 150 mM NaCl and 1 mM DTT.

Uniformly 15N or 13C, 15N-labeled proteins were expressed by growing E. coli host cells in M9 minimal medium containing 1 g/L 15NH4Cl or 1 g/L 15NH4Cl and 2 g/L 13C-glucose. 2H, 15N-labeled proteins were expressed by growing E. coli host cells in M9 minimal medium in 2H2O containing 1 g/L 15NH4Cl, 2 g/L 2H-glucose, and 0.2 g/L 2H, 15N-celtone. 2H, 13C, 15N-labeled proteins were expressed by growing E. coli host cells in M9 minimal medium in 2H2O containing 1 g/L 15NH4Cl, 2 g/L 2H, 13C-glucose and 0.2 g/L 2H, 13C, 15N-celtone. These isotopically labeled proteins were purified using a similar procedure as used for non-labeled proteins.

Preparation of FOXO3a-phosphorylated peptides
We purchased the following FOXO3a-phosphorylated peptides (Shanghai Royo Biotech Co., LTD), and dissolved in Milli-Q water for NMR experiments or a buffer containing 20 mM NaPi (pH 7.4), 150 mM NaCl, and 1 mM DTT for ITC experiments.

P1-peptide: RPRSC-pT-WPLQR (FOXO3a residues 27-37, MW = 1478.64)
P2-peptide: RRRAV-pS-MDNSN (FOXO3a residues 248-258, MW = 1384.43)

Preparation of DNA and fluorescein-labeled DNA
We purchased the following oligonucleotides containing the consensus FOXO binding sequence (DBE sequence) (Eurofins and Thermo Fisher) and prepared dsDNA:
sense: 5′-CTATGTAAACAAC-3′,
antisense: 5′-GTTGTTTACATAG-3′ (DBE),
and fluorescein-antisense: 5′-fluorescein-GTTGTTTACATAG-3′.
The molar concentrations of oligonucleotides were evaluated by measuring the UV absorption at 260 nm based on Lambert–Beer’s law:
c = Abs260 / εl
where c is the molar concentration of the oligonucleotide, Abs260 and ε is the UV absorption and the molar extinction coefficient value at a wavelength of 260 nm, respectively, and l is the optical path length of 1 cm. ε was calculated using the nearest neighbor method34,35. εsense was 133140 and εantisense was 132180. εfluorescein-antisense was calculated as 153080 as the sum of εantisense 132180 and εfluorescein 2090036. Sense and anti-sense were mixed in 1 equivalent each and annealed by decreasing the temperature from 100 °C to 25 °C at 1 °C/min in a buffer containing 20 mM NaPi (pH 6.4) and 150 mM NaCl for ITC experiments, 20 mM NaPi (pH 6.4) and 100 mM NaCl for NMR experiments, or 10 mM Tris-HCl (pH 7.5), 100 mM NaCl, and 1 mM EDTA for FSEC experiments.

SEC-MALS analysis
20 μL of the complex of dpFOXO3a–14-3-3ζ dimer (12.3 mg/mL) was loaded onto WTC-030S5 column (Wyatt) pre-equilibrated with 20 mM Tris (pH 7.5), 300 mM NaCl, 1 mM DTT at 0.4 mL/min at room temperature. DAWN HELEOS II detector (Wyatt) was used to measure MALS, while the RH-101 detector (Shodex) was used to detect refractive index. Data analysis was performed using ASTRA 6.1.7 software (Wyatt) with a dn/dc value of 0.185 mL/g. The samples of dpFOXO3a (8.5 mg/mL) and 14-3-3ζ (8.3 mg/mL) were also analyzed in the same way.

ITC experiments
The binding of 14-3-3ζ or DNA to each FOXO3a was measured by ITC37 using MicroCal PEAQ-ITC (Malvern Instruments). All experiments were performed at 30 °C.

In a buffer containing 20 mM NaPi (pH 7.4), 150 mM NaCl and 1 mM DTT, dpFOXO3a (49 μM and 114 μM) was titrated with the DNA (4.8 μM) or 14-3-3ζ dimer (9.4 μM). pT32-FOXO3a (S253A) (46 μM), pS253-FOXO3a (T32A) (49 μM), and the CTD (48 μM) were titrated with the DNA (4.8 μM, 4.3 μM, 4.5 μM), respectively.

The significant heat exchanges of the 14-3-3ζ binding to pT32-FOXO3a (S253A) and pS253-FOXO3a (T32A) were not observed in the phosphate buffer, although their bindings were observed in FSEC experiments. Therefore, we performed the ITC experiments in a buffer containing 20 mM HEPES (pH 7.5), 150 mM NaCl and 1 mM DTT. In the HEPES buffer, dpFOXO3a (138 μM), P1-peptide (988 μM), and P2-peptide (989 μM) were titrated with 14-3-3ζ dimer (12 μM, 48 μM, and 49 μM), respectively. 14-3-3ζ dimer (150 μM and 88 μM) was titrated with pT32-FOXO3a (S253A) (30 μM) and pS253-FOXO3a (T32A) (18 μM), respectively.

The heats of the injectant dilution were determined by titration of the injectant into the buffer, followed by subtraction from the row titration data before analysis using MicroCal PEAQ-ITC Analysis Software (Malvern), except for the P1-peptide–14-3-3ζ experiment in the HEPES buffer. A ‘One Set of Sites’ model was applied for curve fitting. Thermodynamic parameters with error values were calculated from the fitted data.

FSEC analysis
All experiments were conducted at 4 °C using EnrichTM SEC 650 10×300 Column (BIO-RAD) with LC-20AD, DGU-20A5, SIL-20A, CBM-20A, and RF-20A XS (SHIMADZU). The fluorescein-labeled DNA was detected by the fluorescence of fluorescein (λex = 465 nm, λem = 540 nm) and the proteins were detected by that of tryptophan (λex = 280 nm, λem = 350 nm). The running buffer contains 20 mM NaPi (pH 7.4), 150 mM NaCl, and 1 mM DTT, and the flow rate is 0.5 mL/min. Before analyzing the mixture of dpFOXO3a, the DNA, and 14-3-3ζ, 1% BSA was applied to suppress the sample adsorption. Then, the buffer was run to remove excess BSA.

In FSEC experiments for the competition of dpFOXO3a, the DNA, and 14-3-3ζ, the sample concentrations were as follows: dpFOXO3a (10 μM), DNA (11 μM), and 14-3-3ζ dimer (0, 2.5, 5, 7.5, 10, 12.5 μM). Each experiment was repeated independently 3–4 times on the same sample (technical replicates). In FSEC experiments with pT32-FOXO3a (S253A) and pS253-FOXO3a (T32A), the sample concentrations were as follows: pT32-FOXO3a (S253A) (10 μM), pS253-FOXO3a (T32A) (10 μM), DNA (15 μM), and 14-3-3ζ dimer (10 μM). FOXO3a (10 μM) was mixed with the DNA (11 μM) and 14-3-3ζ dimer (10 μM). The full FSEC-based competition analysis for pS253-FOXO3a (T32A) (10 μM) and DNA (15 μM) titrated 0, 2.5, 5, 7.5, 10, 12.5, 20, 40 μM 14-3-3ζ dimer. Measurements were performed in triplicate on the same sample (technical replicates). Competition analyses using 14-3-3ζ mutants were conducted with dpFOXO3a (10 μM), DNA (11 μM), and 14-3-3ζ mutants dimer (10 μM).

The fluorescence intensity was normalized using the following equations:
Fnorm = (Fn - F0eq) / (F1.25eq - F0eq)
where Fn is the fluorescence intensity observed with the addition of n equivalent amount of 14-3-3ζ dimer. The competition between 14-3-3ζ and the DNA for dpFOXO3a were simulated using the following equation:
Kd = [A][B]/[A-B]
where [A] is the concentration of 14-3-3ζ or the DNA, [B] is that of dpFOXO3a, and [A–B] is that of the 14-3-3ζ–dpFOXO3a complex or DNA–dpFOXO3a complex. The concentration of the DNA (11 μM), that of dpFOXO3a (10 μM), and the Kd value for DNA–dpFOXO3a binding were considered as constants. The concentration of 14-3-3ζ dimer and the Kd value for 14-3-3ζ–dpFOXO3a binding were as variables. The simulations were most consistent with the FSEC results when the 14-3-3ζ stoichiometry was set to 0.8.

NMR analysis
Data were collected on Bruker Avance 600 and 800, or Ascend Evo 1.0 GHz spectrometers (Billerica) equipped with TXI or TCI probes. All spectra were processed using Bruker TopSpin 4.2.0 software, and data were analyzed using Sparky (T.D. Goddard and D.G. Kneller, Sparky 3.190, University of California). All experiments were performed at 303 K in the buffer containing 20 mM NaPi (pH 6.4), 100 mM NaCl, 1 mM DTT, and 8–10% 2H2O.

The backbone NMR resonances for dpFOXO3a and CTD were assigned based on our previous report (the accession number of the BMRB: 26350 and 26346)23. The assignments of the backbone NMR resonances for 2H, 13C, 15N-labeled 14-3-3ζ were archived using HNCO, HNCA, HN(CO)CA, HN(CA)CO, HNCACB, 1H-15N NOESY-TROSY experiments, 1H-15N HSQC with Arg, Phe, Leu, or Met-selective 15N-labeled 14-3-3ζ, and the assignment data of 14-3-3ζ ΔC12 (residues 1-233) (BMRB: 25231)25. We deposited the assignments of 14-3-3ζ to the BMRB (accession number: 26348).

2H, 15N-labeled dpFOXO3a (169 μM) and 2H, 15N-labeled CTD (150 μM) were titrated with unlabeled 14-3-3ζ dimer and 2H, 15N-labeled CTD (150 μM) was also titrated with T215A/L216A/Q219A/R222A 14-3-3ζ mutant. 2H, 15N-labeled 14-3-3ζ dimer (82 μM, 100 μM, 128 μM, 92 μM, and 123 μM) was titrated with unlabeled dpFOXO3a, pNTD, pCTD, P2-peptide, and CTD, respectively. The experiments were monitored using a 1H-15N TROSY spectrum. Chemical shift changes were calculated using the following equation:
Δδ = sqrt(Δδ1H^2 + (Δδ15N / 6.5)^2)
where Δδ1H and Δδ15N are the chemical shift changes in the 1H and 15N dimensions, respectively.

When unlabeled 14-3-3ζ was titrated to 2H, 15N-labeled CTD, and unlabeled CTD to 2H, 15N-labeled 14-3-3ζ, the chemical shift changes of the signals were observed as the fast exchange regime. Therefore, the dissociation constant and the stoichiometry of the CTD and 14-3-3ζ were calculated from the chemical shift changes using the following equation:
Δδ = Δδmax * (x + [P]tot + Kd - sqrt((x + [P]tot + Kd)^2 - 4 * x * [P]tot)) / (2 * [P]tot)
where Δδmax is maximum of the chemical shift changes, [P]tot is the concentration of the host protein, x is that of the ligand protein, and n is the stoichiometry. Curve fitting was performed using Origin 2015. NMR cross-saturation experiments were performed with 222 μM 2H, 15N-labeled 14-3-3ζ in complex with 1.25 equivalent of dpFOXO3a, containing 20% 2H2O/80% 2H2O and selectively saturated dpFOXO3a by irradiating the aliphatic proton resonances, using the mlevsp180.p30 decoupling program. The saturation frequency was set at 1.0 ppm, and the saturation time was set to 1.0 s.

Competition analysis of 126 μM 2H, 15N-labeled dpFOXO3a with 1.1 equivalents of DNA and 1.5 equivalents of 14-3-3ζ dimer were monitored using 1H-15N TROSY spectrum at 600 and 800 MHz. The diluted sample (16 μM dpFOXO3a with 18 μM DNA plus 24 μM 14-3-3ζ) was also monitored using 1H-15N TROSY spectrum at 600 MHz. NMR samples were analyzed by gel filtration using SuperdexTM 200 increase 10/300 GL (Cytiva).

In the magnetic field- and temperature-dependent analyses, we prepared 209 μM 2H, 15N-labeled 14-3-3ζ with 1.25 equivalent of dpFOXO3a and measured 1H-15N TROSY spectra at 1 GHz at different temperatures: 303 K, 298 K, and 293 K.

### Reviewer 1

The manuscript "14-3-3ζ interacts with DNA binding domain of FOXO3a and competitively dissociates DNA by dual motif tethering" by Enomoto et al. studies the FOXO3a/14-3-3 ζ /DNA ternary system by ITC, FSEC and NMR. This is another example of a protein fully displacing DNA in spite of similar affinities. At first glance, this is counter-intuitive, but it adds to a growing number of systems where such behavior has been identified.

In principle I think the manuscript is scientifically sound and of broad interest to warrant publication in Nature Communications. However, I would request additional experiments and edits from the authors as follows:
1) Can the authors confirm their key finding (full displacement of DNA by an equimolar amount of 14-3-3 to dpFOXO3a) by a method different from FSEC? FSEC is not an equilibrium method, and on/off kinetics may play a role and confound the analysis. Could the authors demonstrate this key finding e.g. by NMR?
2) The affinity of 14-3-3 to FOXO3a is 2-fold higher than the affinity of DNA to FOXO3a, hence displacement of DNA by 14-3-3 is only quantitatively, but not qualitatively, surprising. The authors also have the monophosphorylated system pS253-FOXO3a (T32A) which binds much weaker to 14-3-3 but still partially displaces DNA. Could the authors please perform a titration and present the full competition analysis with pS253-FOXO3a (T32A), as they did for dpFOXO3a ?
3) Please define the term “competitiveness” briefly and verbally in the main text, without the equation used in the Supplemental Information
4) Please move Supplementary Table 2 to the main text, as it is important to understand the argument.
5) The Kd value of 5–30 μM for the FOXO3a –14-3-3ζ interaction is quite confusing. Which FOXO3a construct was used for this experiment? I assume it is only the DBD, but this is not clearly stated, and why does the paragraph then often refer to the protein as dpFOXO3a ?
6) The Figure numbering is off for several Figures
Points 1 and 2 will need additional experiments, but I feel only these additional experiments will make the paper really valuable for publication in Nature Communications.

### Reviewer 2

Foxo3a is a well-established tumor-suppressive transcription factor that activates the expression of various anti-proliferative and pro-apoptotic genes. The 14-3-3 protein binds to diphosphorylated Foxo3a at threonine 32 (T32) and serine 253 (S253), inhibiting its DNA-binding activity. However, the precise mechanism of this inhibition remains unclear.
This manuscript investigates the potential mechanism by which 14-3-3 binding displaces Foxo3a from DNA, despite the phosphorylation sites of Foxo3a being distant from the DNA-binding domain (DBD). Using a combination of biophysical approaches—FSEC, ITC, and NMR—the authors propose that 14-3-3 interacts not only with the phosphorylated sites but also directly with the DBD of Foxo3a. They further suggest a two-step mechanism: initial binding of 14-3-3 to site P1 of Foxo3a forms a ternary complex, followed by the binding of a second 14-3-3 molecule that facilitates dissociation of Foxo3a from DNA.
Major Points for Consideration:
1. Novelty of the Findings:
The novelty of the findings needs to be clearly demonstrated. A similar study was published in ACS Omega (Vol. 7, Issue 28, July 5, 2022), titled “Structure of a 14-3-3ε:FOXO3a-pS253 Phosphopeptide Complex Reveals 14-3-3 Isoform-Specific Binding of Forkhead Box Class O Transcription Factor (FOXO) Phosphoproteins.” That paper reported that 14-3-3ε binding induces conformational changes that reposition critical arginine residues in Foxo3a, reducing its DNA-binding affinity.
While the current manuscript presents NMR-based data identifying additional critical residues upon protein interaction, the novelty and functional significance of these residues in regulating Foxo3a's DNA-binding activity have not been fully validated. For instance, site-directed mutagenesis of 14-3-3 residues in contact with the Foxo3a DBD could provide direct evidence of their role in Foxo3a displacement. Crosslinking experiments using chemical or UV crosslinkers, followed by identification of the crosslinked amino acids, would also significantly strengthen the conclusions.
Additionally, the NMR data indicate several residues involved in direct contact between the proteins. However, it remains unclear to an NMR nonspecialist whether these residues reflect direct interactions or result from allosteric conformational changes. This distinction should be clarified.
The weak binding of DBD to 14-3-3ζ was indicated only by NMR chemical shift and affinity measurements (Page 8, The Kd value for the DBD – 14-3-3ζ interaction was calculated to be 5–30 μM). However, without high-resolution structural data (such as crystal structures or cryo-EM) it is hard to support the mechanistic conclusions of this manuscript. Furthermore, the dynamic exchange model was primarily based on NMR signal splitting phenomena (e.g., splitting of the E202 signal into A and B, Figure 9a), but it was not validated through blocking exchange with mutants or real-time kinetic experiments, nor supported by structural data. Moreover, the hypothesis that DBD rapidly exchanges between 14-3-3ζ dimers was not substantiated by resolving the complex structure with individual monomers or through direct functional experiments. These gaps may lead to conclusions that exceed the scope of data support.
2. Figure Mislabeling:
The manuscript contains mislabeled or missing figure numbers (e.g., no Figure 6), leading to confusion and hindering the review process. This oversight suggests a lack of thorough proofreading prior to submission and should be corrected to maintain clarity and professionalism.
Minor Points:
1. Kd Determination Using Truncated Protein:
The dissociation constant (Kd) was determined using a truncated version of Foxo3a (residues 1–284). It is important to address whether this truncated construct behaves similarly to the full-length protein in Kd values. Is there any evidence that the full-length and truncated forms have comparable Kd values?
2. Incorrect Literature Citation:
On page 5, line 96, the cited papers focus on Foxo4 rather than Foxo3a. Please ensure that the references are relevant and specific to the subject of the manuscript.
3. Limited Evidence for Direct DBD Interaction:
The proposed direct binding of 14-3-3 to the DBD of Foxo3a and the suggested hybrid binding model are currently supported solely by NMR data, which were obtained using the truncated protein and peptides. This weakens the overall conclusion. Crosslinking experiments and site-specific mutagenesis would provide more robust support for these claims.
4. Inadequate Comparison with Existing Studies:
The authors only mentioned the similar mechanism of FOXO4 but did not conduct a detailed comparison of the phosphorylation site specificity, DBD structural differences, or functional regulatory similarities and differences between FOXO3a and FOXO4, leading to limited innovation in this study. It is recommended to include a structural and functional comparison between FOXO3a and FOXO4 in the Discussion section and to discuss other subtypes of the 14-3-3 family.

### Reviewer 3

I co-reviewed this manuscript with one of the reviewers who provided the listed reports. This is part of the Nature Communications initiative to facilitate training in peer review and to provide appropriate recognition for Early Career Researchers who co-review manuscripts.

reviewer_updating.input:
You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications.

You previously reviewed this paper and raised several concerns. The authors have now submitted a revised manuscript along with a detailed point-by-point response. Your task is to write your updated review after carefully reading:
  1. The revised paper
  2. Your original Round 1 review
  3. The authors' point-by-point response

In your updated review, explicitly state which concerns have been adequately addressed and which remain outstanding. Be specific.

## Paper

## Abstract

In cancer cells, Ras protein mutations activate a signaling cascade that phosphorylates kinases, transcription, and translation factors, driving cancer cell proliferation. One such factor, FOXO3a, promotes apoptosis-related gene transcription. However, in many cancer cells, FOXO3a is phosphorylated and is bound to 14-3-3ζ at phosphorylation sites. The 14-3-3ζ binding displaces phosphorylated FOXO3a from DNA, suppressing apoptosis. Since the phosphorylation sites are far from the DNA-binding domain (DBD) of FOXO3a, the mechanism of displacement remains unclear. Using isothermal titration calorimetry and fluorescence-detection size-exclusion chromatography, we find that 14-3-3ζ strongly displaces DNA from di-phosphorylated FOXO3a (dpFOXO3a), despite similar dissociation constants for dpFOXO3a–14-3-3ζ and dpFOXO3a–DNA. Nuclear magnetic resonance data identify weak, but direct binding of 14-3-3ζ to the DBD, suggesting direct competition. These findings suggest that 14-3-3ζ enhances its competitive ability by dual tethering to the DBD of FOXO3a via phosphorylation sites, effectively displacing DNA.

---

## Introduction

In cancer cells, Ras proteins are activated by mutations independently of upstream regulators, initiating a signaling cascade. This cascade consists of the sequential phosphorylation of three or more kinases, ultimately leading to the phosphorylation of effector proteins involved in transcription and translation1. Phosphorylation up- or down-regulates effector protein function, causing uncontrolled cell proliferation, apoptosis evasion, invasion, and metastasis1. One such effector protein is FOXO3a, which is a transcriptional activator of genes encoding a number of apoptosis-related proteins such as Bim and FasL that inhibit the cell proliferation2–4. However, in tumor cells transcriptional activity of FOXO3a is inhibited upon its phosphorylation and subsequent binding of an adaptor protein, 14-3-3ζ, resulting in cancer progression via cancer cell apoptosis suppression2.

FOXO3a (a 71 kDa protein consisting of 673 residues) is a member of the forkhead box (FOX) protein family. FOXO3a comprises a DNA-binding domain (DBD), also called the forkhead domain (residues 157–250), and intrinsically disordered regions in the N- and C-terminals (Fig. 1)5,6. The DBD binds to specific DNA sequences (referred to as FOXO-responsive elements, FREs), triggering apoptosis-related gene transcription. In tumor cells, FOXO3a is phosphorylated at three residues (T32, S253, and S315) in the intrinsically disordered regions by an upstream kinase, AKT. Subsequently, its transcriptional activity is inhibited by the binding of an adaptor protein, 14-3-3ζ2, which is highly expressed in cancer cells7.

14-3-3ζ, a member of the 14-3-3 protein family, is a 245-residue acidic protein, consisting of nine α-helices. 14-3-3ζ exists and functions as an axisymmetric dimer8. 14-3-3ζ binds to the Ser/Thr-phosphorylated motifs in its target proteins and prevents their dephosphorylation, prolonging the functional regulation by phosphorylation9. 14-3-3ζ recognizes two phosphorylated motifs in the N-terminal region of FOXO3a (P1: RPRSC-pT-WPLQR, P2: RRRAV-pS-MDNSN)2,10,11. Upon binding to the phosphorylated FOXO3a, 14-3-3ζ dissociates FOXO3a from FREs, thereby inhibiting its transcriptional activity2,12,13. Furthermore, 14-3-3ζ masks the nuclear localization signal (RRR) of FOXO3a located within the P2 site, facilitating the export of FOXO3a from the nucleus to the cytoplasm14,15. In the cytoplasm, FOXO3a is ubiquitinated and subject to degradation16,17. Consequently, FOXO3a-mediated apoptosis is suppressed, leading to malignant cancer transformation. Reportedly, cancer cell apoptosis is enhanced by inhibiting the interaction between phosphorylated FOXO3a and 14-3-3ζ18. Therefore, inhibiting the interaction is a viable target for anticancer drugs. Although understanding the mechanism of action is important, it remains unknown how the 14-3-3ζ binding dissociates FOXO3a from its target DNA sequence, as the 14-3-3ζ binding sites, P1 and P2, located remotely from the DBD.

This dissociation mechanism has been mainly studied using FOXO4, which has a similar structure to a member of the FOXO family19. FOXO4 has high sequence identity with FOXO3a at P1 (100%), P2 (86%), and the DBD (83%), supporting the assumption that their interaction modes with DNA and 14-3-3ζ are highly similar, and thus that Kd values of FOXO4 provide a reliable reference for FOXO3a. A previous study12 showed that 14-3-3ζ dissociates di-phosphorylated FOXO4 (dpFOXO4) from the DNA with the human insulin response element (hIRE). This result was attributed to the difference in dissociation constants (Kds), which were reported to be 30 nM for dpFOXO4–14-3-3ζ and 500 nM for dpFOXO4–hIRE. However, as the consensus DNA sequence recognized by the FOXO family (e.g., daf-16 binding element, DBE)20 has higher affinity for FOXO3a than for hIRE21, the relative binding affinity of phosphorylated FOXO3a for DBE and 14-3-3ζ should be analyzed quantitatively under the same conditions to conclude that the dissociation is caused by the difference in their Kd values.

In another study, the binding mode of the DBD of FOXO4 and the 14-3-3ζ dimer was deduced based on the distance constraints obtained from fluorescence resonance energy transfer (FRET) experiments using 14-3-3ζ ‘monomeric mutants’ and a FOXO4 fragment, which contained the DBD and was mono-phosphorylated at the P2 site22. However, the direct interaction between the 14-3-3ζ dimer and the DBD within dpFOXO4 has not yet been experimentally observed.

Here, we quantitatively analyze the binding affinity and competition of di-phosphorylated FOXO3a (dpFOXO3a), DNA, and 14-3-3ζ using isothermal titration calorimetry (ITC) and fluorescence-detection size-exclusion chromatography (FSEC). In addition, we execute NMR analyses on the interaction between dpFOXO3a and 14-3-3ζ. Based on these results, we propose a mechanism of the FOXO3a dissociation from DNA by the 14-3-3ζ binding.

---

## Results

14-3-3ζ binds to dpFOXO3a and completely dissociates DNA from the dpFOXO3a-DNA complex

We expressed and purified FOXO3a residues 1–284 (hereafter referred to as FOXO3a) containing the DBD and two 14-3-3ζ-binding motifs, each of which possesses a phosphorylation site, T32 in P1 and S253 in P2, respectively, as previously reported (Fig. 1 and Supplementary Fig. 1a)23. Di-phosphorylated FOXO3a (dpFOXO3a) was prepared by phosphorylating FOXO3a using AKT (Supplementary Fig. 2a). The truncated construct FOXO3a (residues 1–284) used in this study is expected to have essentially the same binding affinities to DNA and to 14-3-3ζ as the full-length protein. For DNA binding, the interaction is dominated by the DBD5, and while the transactivation domain (TAD) can compete with DNA for the DBD6,13, the DNA–DBD interaction is strong enough to displace the TAD13. For 14-3-3ζ binding, the recognition of the two phosphorylated motifs (P1 and P2) of FOXO3a is known to be dominant. Isothermal titration calorimetry (ITC) analysis indicated the Kd value of 130 nM for the dpFOXO3a – DNA (DBE sequence, see “Methods” section) interaction (Table 1 and Supplementary Fig. 4a). 14-3-3ζ was also expressed and purified to homogeneity (Supplementary Fig. 1f). Size-exclusion chromatography – multi-angle light scattering (SEC-MALS) analysis indicated that the 14-3-3ζ dimer forms a 1:1 complex with dpFOXO3a (Supplementary Fig. 3). The Kd value for the dpFOXO3a interaction with 14-3-3ζ was 60 nM (Table 1 and Supplementary Fig. 4b), which is ~half that of the interaction with DNA (130 nM). These Kd values, together with binding stoichiometry, are consistent with previous reports for dpFOXO42,12, which has the similar binding mode, indicating that the samples we prepared possessed appropriate binding activities.

First, we quantitatively analyzed the competition between 14-3-3ζ and DNA for binding to dpFOXO3a by fluorescence-detection size-exclusion chromatography (FSEC). The fluorescein-labeling of the DNA duplex containing the DBE sequence enabled selective detection of the DNA based on the fluorescence from the fluorescein moiety, while the proteins (dpFOXO3a and/or 14-3-3ζ) were detected by their tryptophan fluorescence (Fig. 2). When a sample containing 10 μM dpFOXO3a and 11 μM DNA was analyzed by FSEC, the elution profiles showed a peak of the dpFOXO3a–DNA complex at the elution volume of 13.1 mL (Black in Figs. 2a, b). As the increasing amounts of 14-3-3ζ were added to the 1:1 mixture of dpFOXO3a and DNA, the peak height of the dpFOXO3a-bound DNA and free DNA decreased and increased, respectively (Fig. 2a), whereas the peak of DNA-bound dpFOXO3a gradually shifted toward the peak of the dpFOXO3a–14-3-3ζ dimer complex (Fig. 2b). These changes were saturated when one equivalent of the 14-3-3ζ dimer was added. These results indicate that the equimolar amount of 14-3-3ζ completely dissociated dpFOXO3a from the DNA.

We then simulated the competitiveness of 14-3-3ζ against the DNA on dpFOXO3a. Here, ‘competitiveness’ refers to the relative ability of 14-3-3ζ or DNA to bind to dpFOXO3a under the same concentration conditions. In quantitative terms, this can be expressed as the ratio of concentration to the dissociation constant (concentration/Kd), as described in the supplementary discussion. The simulation results (Figs. 2c–e) showed that the experimental FSEC results (solid lines) were not explained by the factor of two (dashed black lines), which is based on the reciprocal Kd ratio calculated using the Kd values obtained by ITC (Kd (dpFOXO3a – DNA) / Kd (dpFOXO3a – 14-3-3ζ) = 130/60) (Supplementary Fig. 4). However, the FSEC results are well explained by assuming the factor of 100 (thick dashed lines), demonstrating that 14-3-3ζ possesses ~100-fold competitiveness over DNA for dpFOXO3a. As 100-fold higher competitiveness is notably higher than the two-fold, which is expected from the experimental Kd values, an unknown mechanism seems to underlie the high competitiveness. On the other hand, NMR analysis of [2H, 15N]-dpFOXO3a bound to DNA upon addition of 14-3-3ζ showed that most signals did not change; however, the signals corresponding to P1 and P2 disappeared or shifted in a manner identical to that observed when 14-3-3ζ bound to dpFOXO3a in the absence of DNA (Supplementary Fig. 5a, b, and 6a). This indicates that 14-3-3ζ can bind to dpFOXO3a at the P1 and P2 sites even while dpFOXO3a remains associated with DNA. SEC of the same sample showed that this ternary complex was unstable, with ~74% of DNA free at 126 μM protein concentration and ~91% free at 16 μM (Supplementary Fig. 5c, d, 6b, and c), indicating strong concentration dependence.

14-3-3ζ binding to pS253 of dpFOXO3a mainly contributes to the DNA dissociation, whereas pT32 binding is necessary for complete DNA dissociation

To investigate the functional role of the phosphorylation sites, P1 and P2, of dpFOXO3a in the 14-3-3ζ binding and the high competitiveness against the DNA, we prepared the mono-phosphorylated mutants, pT32-FOXO3a(S253A) and pS253-FOXO3a(T32A), and analyzed their interactions with 14-3-3ζ and DNA. ITC analyses indicated that the binding affinities of these mutants for the DNA were similar to the wild type (Table 1 and Supplementary Fig. 7a, b), while those for 14-3-3ζ were weaker than the wild type protein but sufficiently high for these FSEC analyses at the concentrations of 10 μM (Table 1 and Supplementary Fig. 8b, c). When the equimolar mixture of pT32-FOXO3a(S253A), DNA, and 14-3-3ζ dimer was applied to FSEC, the elution volume of the peak of the protein-bound DNA slightly shifted from 13.1 to 13.0 mL and the peak shape was broadened, while the peak position and height of the unbound DNA did not change (Fig. 3a). In the meantime, the elution volume of the peak observed by the tryptophan fluorescence corresponded to the protein-bound DNA at 12.9 mL (Fig. 3b). These results indicate that 14-3-3ζ binds to the pT32-FOXO3a(S253A)–DNA complex, forming a ternary complex.

In contrast, when the equimolar mixture of the pS253-FOXO3a(T32A), DNA, and 14-3-3ζ dimer was applied, the peak height of the protein-bound DNA decreased by 42%, whereas that of unbound DNA increased by more than two-fold, indicating that the DNA partially dissociated from pS253-FOXO3a(T32A). Simultaneously, the peak observed by the tryptophan fluorescence shifted forward (Figs. 3c, d), demonstrating that 14-3-3ζ binds to pS253-FOXO3a(T32A). The full FSEC-based competition analysis revealed that at one equivalent of 14-3-3ζ dimer, only ~50% of the DNA complex was dissociated, compared with ~95% for dpFOXO3a, and even with four equivalents dissociation reached only ~83% (Supplementary Fig. 9).

Notably, the P1 site containing pT32 has higher binding affinity for 14-3-3ζ (Kd = 1.2 μM) than the P2 site containing pS253 (Kd = 21 μM), as confirmed by the ITC experiments using phosphorylated peptides, P1-peptide (RPRSC-pT-WPLQR), and P2-peptide (RRRAV-pS-MDNSN) (Table 1 and Supplementary Fig. 8).

We also performed this competition analysis using unphosphorylated FOXO3a as a control. Figure 3e shows that there were no changes on the elution profile of the DNA, while the peak for 14-3-3ζ appeared on the DNA-bound FOXO3a when one equivalent of 14-3-3ζ dimer was added (Fig. 3f), indicating that the phosphorylation at both two motifs of FOXO3a is necessary for the 14-3-3ζ binding and DNA dissociation.

Altogether, these FSEC results using di-/mono-phosphorylated FOXO3a, DNA, and 14-3-3ζ suggest that the binding of the P2 site to 14-3-3ζ mainly contributes to the DNA dissociation from dpFOXO3a. However, P1 site binding, which has a higher affinity than the P2 site, is needed for the full competitiveness against DNA. It remains unclear how 14-3-3ζ binds to both phosphorylation sites, which are located 126- and 11-residue apart from the structural region of the DBD, and facilitates DNA dissociation from the DBD. To elucidate the mechanism, we investigated the dpFOXO3a–14-3-3ζ interaction using nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy.

14-3-3ζ directly interacts with dpFOXO3a at the DNA-binding domain (DBD) and the two phosphorylation motifs

First, we analyzed the NMR spectral changes of dpFOXO3a after adding 14-3-3ζ. The assignments of the backbone resonances of dpFOXO3a in the free state (BMRB: 26350) were described in a previous study23. A series of the 1H-15N transverse relaxation-optimized spectroscopy (TROSY) spectra of uniformly 2H, 15N-labeled dpFOXO3a were observed upon sequential additions of unlabeled 14-3-3ζ (Fig. 4). As the added amount of 14-3-3ζ increased, 66 signals disappeared, and 54 new signals appeared, suggesting that the spectral changes occurred apparently in a slow exchange manner. The changes almost saturated when one equivalent of the 14-3-3ζ dimer was added.

Next, we analyzed the chemical shift perturbation to identify the regions in dpFOXO3a affected by the 14-3-3ζ binding (Fig. 4c). The backbone assignments of the DBD of dpFOXO3a bound to 14-3-3ζ were transferred from those of C-terminal domain (CTD) construct of FOXO3a (residues 141-284, Fig. 1), which contains the DBD together with the C-terminal unstructured tail, rather than the DBD alone (Supplementary Fig. 10). Consequently, the dpFOXO3a residues that showed chemical shift changes above 0.03 ppm were not only around the P1 and P2 sites, but also around the helix 3 of the DBD (Fig. 4c). Mapping of the affected residues onto the DBD structure revealed that these residues were localized to one side of the DBD that includes helix 3 (Figs. 4c, d). These results suggest that in addition to the P1 and P2 sites, the region around the helix 3 on the DBD is the 14-3-3ζ-binding interface, which overlap well with the DNA-binding interface in the crystal structure of the DBD–DNA complex (Fig. 4e)24. NMR analysis monitoring the spectral changes of the CTD upon additions of 14-3-3ζ confirmed the 14-3-3ζ-binding region on the DBD of dpFOXO3a (Supplementary Fig. 10c–e). Notably, the curve fitting of the chemical shift changes of [2H, 15N]-CTD was established by the 14-3-3ζ titration that resulted in a Kd value of 5–30 μM for the DBD–14-3-3ζ interaction (Supplementary Fig. 10b).

Grooves of the 14-3-3ζ dimer accommodate the two phosphorylation motifs of dpFOXO3a and the upper regions of the grooves interact with the DBD

We analyzed the NMR spectral changes of uniformly 2H, 15N-labeled 14-3-3ζ, upon the sequential additions of unlabeled dpFOXO3a. Backbone resonances have been assigned for full length 14-3-3ζ for 211 of the total 244 observable residues (86%, BMRB: 26348) by a series of triple resonance experiments with reference to the previously reported assignments for the residues 1–23325 (Supplementary Fig. 11). In the free state of 14-3-3ζ, each residue provides only one peak, indicating that the 14-3-3ζ dimer possesses a symmetric structure in the NMR timescale.

Through sequential additions of dpFOXO3a, 116 signals of 14-3-3ζ disappeared from 1H-15N TROSY spectra, and 133 new signals appeared in a slow exchange manner. The signal changes almost saturated when one equivalent of dpFOXO3a was added to the 14-3-3ζ dimer (Fig. 5a). The increase in the number of signals is mainly due to splitting of the signals as shown in Fig. 5b. The splitting reflects that the 14-3-3ζ dimer is asymmetric in the complex with dpFOXO3a (Fig. 5b), where each protomer of the 14-3-3ζ dimer binds to the P1 or P2 sites of dpFOXO3a, respectively, which possess different amino acid sequences. Establishing the backbone assignments of 14-3-3ζ in the dpFOXO3a-bound state by triple resonance experiments was difficult, due to the line broadening and low sensitivity arising from high molecular mass of the complex (ca. 90 kDa) as well as the signal splitting caused by the asymmetry. Therefore, we evaluated whether each signal of 14-3-3ζ in the free state is affected or not by the addition of dpFOXO3a. The signals whose intensities decreased to 15% or less with the addition of 1.5 equivalents of dpFOXO3a were judged as the affected residues. Mapping of the affected residues indicates that these residues lie not only in the grooves to which the P1 and P2 sites bind, but also in the upper regions of the grooves formed by the helices 8–9 (Figs. 5c, d), suggesting that these upper regions of 14-3-3ζ interact with the dpFOXO3a regions other than the phosphorylated sites, P1 and P2. In addition, the spectral overlay of 14-3-3ζ upon binding to dpFOXO3a with those upon binding to the N-terminal unstructured region upstream of the DBD that is phosphorylated at T32 (referred to as pNTD containing the P1 site) and with those upon binding to the P2-peptide, showed that many signals with pNTD or the P2-peptide overlapped those with dpFOXO3a but 18 and 44 signals in the pNTD-bound state and P2-peptide-bound state, respectively, did not overlap with those in the dpFOXO3a-bound state (Supplementary Fig. 12a). These residues clustered on the 14-3-3ζ surface formed by its helices 8–9 (Supplementary Fig. 12b and c). These spectral differences were likely caused by the DBD that exists only in dpFOXO3a, neither in pNTD nor in the P2-peptide.

Based on these results, we hypothesized that this upper region of 14-3-3ζ interacts with the DBD of dpFOXO3a. To confirm the hypothesis, we analyzed the changes in 1H-15N TROSY spectra of uniformly 2H, 15N-labeled 14-3-3ζ, upon the sequential additions of the unlabeled CTD, which consists of the DBD and the C-terminal tail (Fig. 6). The chemical shift changes were observed in a fast exchange manner, enabling the assignments of the CTD-bound state by tracking the chemical shift changes (Fig. 6b). The residues whose chemical shifts changed more than 0.045 ppm with the addition of 2.5 equivalent of the CTD were clustered on the upper sites of the grooves of 14-3-3ζ (Figs. 6c, d). Given that the DBD in dpFOXO3a interacts with 14-3-3ζ (Fig. 4), we conclude that these upper sites of the grooves (helices 8–9) are the DBD-binding regions. From the observed chemical shift changes, the Kd value for the 14-3-3ζ binding to the CTD was calculated to be ca. 10 μM (Fig. 6b).

However, CSP identifies residues whose local chemical environment changes upon binding, which can result from either direct contact or conformational changes. To obtain direct evidence for DBD–14-3-3ζ interaction beyond CSP mapping, we performed NMR cross-saturation experiments, which selectively detect residues in close spatial proximity (~5 Å) to dpFOXO3a. This analysis identified specific contact residues on 14-3-3ζ, several of which are located outside the canonical phospho-motif binding groove and positioned to interact with the DBD (Fig. 7).

Quadruple-alanine mutants targeting these sites (D197A/E198A/E202A/D204A or T215A/L216A/Q219A/R222A) showed no reduction in DNA displacement ability in FSEC assays (Supplementary Fig. 13), consistent with a broad interaction interface in which partial disruption does not abolish binding. In contrast, NMR spectral changes of [2H, 15N]-CTD titrated with the T215A/L216A/Q219A/R222A 14-3-3ζ mutant demonstrated that signals, mainly in helix 3, shifted in a different manner or decreased in intensity compared with the titration using wild type 14-3-3ζ. The titration with the D197A/E198A/E202A/D204A mutant was not possible because the sample precipitated and could not be concentrated sufficiently for NMR analysis. Together, these NMR data strongly suggest that the helix 3 of DBD directly interacts with the residues around T215/L216/Q219/R222 of 14-3-3ζ (Supplementary Fig. 14).

DBD undergoes exchange between protomer 1- and 2-bound states in the dpFOXO3a and 14-3-3ζ dimer complex

Some signals of the residues at the DBD interaction site (helices 8–9) of 14-3-3ζ split into two signals (hereafter referred to as signals A and B) when dpFOXO3a was added, reflecting the asymmetry of the 14-3-3ζ dimer, where two protomers bind to P1 and P2, respectively. Then, to assign the split signals whether it is from the P1-bound protomer or P2-bound protomer, we prepared three types of symmetric dimers, in which both protomers are bound to pNTD (N-terminal unstructured region containing P1), pCTD (DBD and C-terminal unstructured region containing P2), or the P2-peptide. Notably, neither signal (A) nor (B) for E202 in the dpFOXO3a-bound state overlapped with the corresponding signals in the symmetric dimers (pNTD-, pCTD-, nor the P2-peptide-bound states) (Fig. 8a). The signal (A) is located in the middle of the signal of pCTD-bound and the P2-peptide-bound states.

It is tempting to speculate that the signal (A) is observed as a result of the fast exchange between the DBD-bound and -unbound states of the P2-bound protomer, where the population of the DBD-bound and -unbound state is almost 1:1. Under this assumption, the signal (B) is regarded as the signal from the P1-bound protomer, which seems due to the fast exchange between the DBD-bound and -unbound states of the P1-bound protomer.

The other five residues in the DBD binding site (D204, T205, E208, S214, and the signal overlapped by E209 and W228) provided split signals, where each signal was broad and distorted (Supplementary Fig. 15a–e), suggesting the multiple states are averaged in a fast-intermediate exchange regime. For the 14-3-3ζ residues in the region not interacting with the DBD, the signal that split into two upon addition of dpFOXO3a overlapped with those upon addition of pNTD, pCTD or the P2-peptide, respectively (e.g., H164) (Supplementary Fig. 15f).

In addition, high-field (1 GHz) NMR experiments provided direct evidences supporting the dynamic exchange of the DBD between the two protomers of the 14-3-3ζ dimer. At 1 GHz, the E202 ‘A’ signal observed in the fast-exchange regime at 800 MHz split into two peaks, consistent with distinct P2-peptide-bound and [P2+DBD]-bound states (Supplementary Fig. 16b, c). The E202 ‘B’ signal remained single at 1 GHz but split into two peaks when the temperature was lowered from 303 K to 293 K, with the ‘A’ peaks merging, indicating that ‘B’ contains both pNTD-bound and [pNTD+DBD]-bound states (Supplementary Fig. 16d, e). These field- and temperature-dependent changes indicate that the DBD dynamically exchanges between the two protomers of the 14-3-3ζ dimer.

Altogether, we propose that in the dpFOXO3a in complex with a 14-3-3ζ dimer, the DBD binds to upper region (helices 8–9) of either protomer of the 14-3-3ζ dimer at one time, where the DBD rapidly exchanges between the two protomers of the 14-3-3ζ dimer (Fig. 8b). The DNA binding interface of the DBD is covered by the upper region of either protomer of 14-3-3ζ most of the time, which competitively inhibits the DNA binding.

## Methods

Protein expression and purification
As previously reported23, we constructed human FOXO3a (residues 1-284), the NTD (residues 1-146) and the CTD (residues 141-284) and purified them. In addition, the mutants FOXO3a (T32A) and FOXO3a (S253A) were generated according to the QuikChange® mutagenesis protocol (Stratagene, La Jolla, CA, USA) using the pGEX-6P-1-FOXO3a plasmid as the template and were purified in the same way as the FOXO3a purification. FOXO3a, FOXO3a (T32A), NTD, and CTD were phosphorylated by AKT23 and FOXO3a (S253A) required the addition of three times the amount of AKT for the phosphorylation. The phosphorylation reaction proceeded completely, confirmed by MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry, using MALDI-8020 spectrometer (SHIMADZU). In the MALDI-TOF MS, α-cyano-4-hydroxycinnamic acid was used as the matrix for FOXO3a, FOXO3a (T32A), FOXO3a (S253A), and the NTD, and sinapinic acid was used for the measurement with CTD. These experiments were performed in a buffer containing 50% acetonitrile and 0.1% TFA. pNTD was additionally purified by reversed-phase chromatography.

The DNA sequence encoding full-length human 14-3-3ζ (residues 1-245), D197A/E198A/E202A/D204A mutant, and T215A/L216A/Q219A/R222A mutant were cloned into the pGEX-6P-1 (Cytiva). The glutathione-S-transferase-fusion proteins were expressed in Escherichia coli C41 (DE3) cells and induced by addition of isopropyl β-D-thiogalactopyranoside at a final concentration of 1 mM for 4 h at 37 °C. The cells were collected by centrifugation and disrupted by sonication in a buffer containing phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) (pH 7.4), 1 M NaCl, 10% glycerol, 1 mM phenylmethanesulfonyl fluoride, 1 mM DTT, and 0.1% polyethylenimine. Cell debris was removed by centrifugation, and the supernatant was purified using a Glutathione-SepharoseTM 4B column (Cytiva) in a buffer containing PBS (pH 7.4), 500 mM NaCl, 1 mM DTT and 10 mM reduced glutathione. Followed by digestion with PreScission Protease (Cytiva), the cleaved glutathione-S-transferase and noncleaved fusion proteins were removed using a Glutathione-SepharoseTM 4B column. The impurities were removed using an anion exchange column (CaptoTM HiRes Q 5/50 GL; Cytiva) in a linear gradient of 0–1 M NaCl in 20 mM Tris-HCl (pH 7.5) and 1 mM DTT. 14-3-3ζ mutants were additionally purified by gel filtration using SuperdexTM 200 increase 10/300 GL (Cytiva) in a buffer containing 20 mM NaPi (pH 7.4), 150 mM NaCl and 1 mM DTT.

Uniformly 15N or 13C, 15N-labeled proteins were expressed by growing E. coli host cells in M9 minimal medium containing 1 g/L 15NH4Cl or 1 g/L 15NH4Cl and 2 g/L 13C-glucose. 2H, 15N-labeled proteins were expressed by growing E. coli host cells in M9 minimal medium in 2H2O containing 1 g/L 15NH4Cl, 2 g/L 2H-glucose, and 0.2 g/L 2H, 15N-celtone. 2H, 13C, 15N-labeled proteins were expressed by growing E. coli host cells in M9 minimal medium in 2H2O containing 1 g/L 15NH4Cl, 2 g/L 2H, 13C-glucose and 0.2 g/L 2H, 13C, 15N-celtone. These isotopically labeled proteins were purified using a similar procedure as used for non-labeled proteins.

Preparation of FOXO3a-phosphorylated peptides
We purchased the following FOXO3a-phosphorylated peptides (Shanghai Royo Biotech Co., LTD), and dissolved in Milli-Q water for NMR experiments or a buffer containing 20 mM NaPi (pH 7.4), 150 mM NaCl, and 1 mM DTT for ITC experiments.

P1-peptide: RPRSC-pT-WPLQR (FOXO3a residues 27-37, MW = 1478.64)
P2-peptide: RRRAV-pS-MDNSN (FOXO3a residues 248-258, MW = 1384.43)

Preparation of DNA and fluorescein-labeled DNA
We purchased the following oligonucleotides containing the consensus FOXO binding sequence (DBE sequence) (Eurofins and Thermo Fisher) and prepared dsDNA:
sense: 5′-CTATGTAAACAAC-3′,
antisense: 5′-GTTGTTTACATAG-3′ (DBE),
and fluorescein-antisense: 5′-fluorescein-GTTGTTTACATAG-3′.
The molar concentrations of oligonucleotides were evaluated by measuring the UV absorption at 260 nm based on Lambert–Beer’s law:
c = Abs260 / εl
where c is the molar concentration of the oligonucleotide, Abs260 and ε is the UV absorption and the molar extinction coefficient value at a wavelength of 260 nm, respectively, and l is the optical path length of 1 cm. ε was calculated using the nearest neighbor method34,35. εsense was 133140 and εantisense was 132180. εfluorescein-antisense was calculated as 153080 as the sum of εantisense 132180 and εfluorescein 2090036. Sense and anti-sense were mixed in 1 equivalent each and annealed by decreasing the temperature from 100 °C to 25 °C at 1 °C/min in a buffer containing 20 mM NaPi (pH 6.4) and 150 mM NaCl for ITC experiments, 20 mM NaPi (pH 6.4) and 100 mM NaCl for NMR experiments, or 10 mM Tris-HCl (pH 7.5), 100 mM NaCl, and 1 mM EDTA for FSEC experiments.

SEC-MALS analysis
20 μL of the complex of dpFOXO3a–14-3-3ζ dimer (12.3 mg/mL) was loaded onto WTC-030S5 column (Wyatt) pre-equilibrated with 20 mM Tris (pH 7.5), 300 mM NaCl, 1 mM DTT at 0.4 mL/min at room temperature. DAWN HELEOS II detector (Wyatt) was used to measure MALS, while the RH-101 detector (Shodex) was used to detect refractive index. Data analysis was performed using ASTRA 6.1.7 software (Wyatt) with a dn/dc value of 0.185 mL/g. The samples of dpFOXO3a (8.5 mg/mL) and 14-3-3ζ (8.3 mg/mL) were also analyzed in the same way.

ITC experiments
The binding of 14-3-3ζ or DNA to each FOXO3a was measured by ITC37 using MicroCal PEAQ-ITC (Malvern Instruments). All experiments were performed at 30 °C.

In a buffer containing 20 mM NaPi (pH 7.4), 150 mM NaCl and 1 mM DTT, dpFOXO3a (49 μM and 114 μM) was titrated with the DNA (4.8 μM) or 14-3-3ζ dimer (9.4 μM). pT32-FOXO3a (S253A) (46 μM), pS253-FOXO3a (T32A) (49 μM), and the CTD (48 μM) were titrated with the DNA (4.8 μM, 4.3 μM, 4.5 μM), respectively.

The significant heat exchanges of the 14-3-3ζ binding to pT32-FOXO3a (S253A) and pS253-FOXO3a (T32A) were not observed in the phosphate buffer, although their bindings were observed in FSEC experiments. Therefore, we performed the ITC experiments in a buffer containing 20 mM HEPES (pH 7.5), 150 mM NaCl and 1 mM DTT. In the HEPES buffer, dpFOXO3a (138 μM), P1-peptide (988 μM), and P2-peptide (989 μM) were titrated with 14-3-3ζ dimer (12 μM, 48 μM, and 49 μM), respectively. 14-3-3ζ dimer (150 μM and 88 μM) was titrated with pT32-FOXO3a (S253A) (30 μM) and pS253-FOXO3a (T32A) (18 μM), respectively.

The heats of the injectant dilution were determined by titration of the injectant into the buffer, followed by subtraction from the row titration data before analysis using MicroCal PEAQ-ITC Analysis Software (Malvern), except for the P1-peptide–14-3-3ζ experiment in the HEPES buffer. A ‘One Set of Sites’ model was applied for curve fitting. Thermodynamic parameters with error values were calculated from the fitted data.

FSEC analysis
All experiments were conducted at 4 °C using EnrichTM SEC 650 10×300 Column (BIO-RAD) with LC-20AD, DGU-20A5, SIL-20A, CBM-20A, and RF-20A XS (SHIMADZU). The fluorescein-labeled DNA was detected by the fluorescence of fluorescein (λex = 465 nm, λem = 540 nm) and the proteins were detected by that of tryptophan (λex = 280 nm, λem = 350 nm). The running buffer contains 20 mM NaPi (pH 7.4), 150 mM NaCl, and 1 mM DTT, and the flow rate is 0.5 mL/min. Before analyzing the mixture of dpFOXO3a, the DNA, and 14-3-3ζ, 1% BSA was applied to suppress the sample adsorption. Then, the buffer was run to remove excess BSA.

In FSEC experiments for the competition of dpFOXO3a, the DNA, and 14-3-3ζ, the sample concentrations were as follows: dpFOXO3a (10 μM), DNA (11 μM), and 14-3-3ζ dimer (0, 2.5, 5, 7.5, 10, 12.5 μM). Each experiment was repeated independently 3–4 times on the same sample (technical replicates). In FSEC experiments with pT32-FOXO3a (S253A) and pS253-FOXO3a (T32A), the sample concentrations were as follows: pT32-FOXO3a (S253A) (10 μM), pS253-FOXO3a (T32A) (10 μM), DNA (15 μM), and 14-3-3ζ dimer (10 μM). FOXO3a (10 μM) was mixed with the DNA (11 μM) and 14-3-3ζ dimer (10 μM). The full FSEC-based competition analysis for pS253-FOXO3a (T32A) (10 μM) and DNA (15 μM) titrated 0, 2.5, 5, 7.5, 10, 12.5, 20, 40 μM 14-3-3ζ dimer. Measurements were performed in triplicate on the same sample (technical replicates). Competition analyses using 14-3-3ζ mutants were conducted with dpFOXO3a (10 μM), DNA (11 μM), and 14-3-3ζ mutants dimer (10 μM).

The fluorescence intensity was normalized using the following equations:
Fnorm = (Fn - F0eq) / (F1.25eq - F0eq)
where Fn is the fluorescence intensity observed with the addition of n equivalent amount of 14-3-3ζ dimer. The competition between 14-3-3ζ and the DNA for dpFOXO3a were simulated using the following equation:
Kd = [A][B]/[A-B]
where [A] is the concentration of 14-3-3ζ or the DNA, [B] is that of dpFOXO3a, and [A–B] is that of the 14-3-3ζ–dpFOXO3a complex or DNA–dpFOXO3a complex. The concentration of the DNA (11 μM), that of dpFOXO3a (10 μM), and the Kd value for DNA–dpFOXO3a binding were considered as constants. The concentration of 14-3-3ζ dimer and the Kd value for 14-3-3ζ–dpFOXO3a binding were as variables. The simulations were most consistent with the FSEC results when the 14-3-3ζ stoichiometry was set to 0.8.

NMR analysis
Data were collected on Bruker Avance 600 and 800, or Ascend Evo 1.0 GHz spectrometers (Billerica) equipped with TXI or TCI probes. All spectra were processed using Bruker TopSpin 4.2.0 software, and data were analyzed using Sparky (T.D. Goddard and D.G. Kneller, Sparky 3.190, University of California). All experiments were performed at 303 K in the buffer containing 20 mM NaPi (pH 6.4), 100 mM NaCl, 1 mM DTT, and 8–10% 2H2O.

The backbone NMR resonances for dpFOXO3a and CTD were assigned based on our previous report (the accession number of the BMRB: 26350 and 26346)23. The assignments of the backbone NMR resonances for 2H, 13C, 15N-labeled 14-3-3ζ were archived using HNCO, HNCA, HN(CO)CA, HN(CA)CO, HNCACB, 1H-15N NOESY-TROSY experiments, 1H-15N HSQC with Arg, Phe, Leu, or Met-selective 15N-labeled 14-3-3ζ, and the assignment data of 14-3-3ζ ΔC12 (residues 1-233) (BMRB: 25231)25. We deposited the assignments of 14-3-3ζ to the BMRB (accession number: 26348).

2H, 15N-labeled dpFOXO3a (169 μM) and 2H, 15N-labeled CTD (150 μM) were titrated with unlabeled 14-3-3ζ dimer and 2H, 15N-labeled CTD (150 μM) was also titrated with T215A/L216A/Q219A/R222A 14-3-3ζ mutant. 2H, 15N-labeled 14-3-3ζ dimer (82 μM, 100 μM, 128 μM, 92 μM, and 123 μM) was titrated with unlabeled dpFOXO3a, pNTD, pCTD, P2-peptide, and CTD, respectively. The experiments were monitored using a 1H-15N TROSY spectrum. Chemical shift changes were calculated using the following equation:
Δδ = sqrt(Δδ1H^2 + (Δδ15N / 6.5)^2)
where Δδ1H and Δδ15N are the chemical shift changes in the 1H and 15N dimensions, respectively.

When unlabeled 14-3-3ζ was titrated to 2H, 15N-labeled CTD, and unlabeled CTD to 2H, 15N-labeled 14-3-3ζ, the chemical shift changes of the signals were observed as the fast exchange regime. Therefore, the dissociation constant and the stoichiometry of the CTD and 14-3-3ζ were calculated from the chemical shift changes using the following equation:
Δδ = Δδmax * (x + [P]tot + Kd - sqrt((x + [P]tot + Kd)^2 - 4 * x * [P]tot)) / (2 * [P]tot)
where Δδmax is maximum of the chemical shift changes, [P]tot is the concentration of the host protein, x is that of the ligand protein, and n is the stoichiometry. Curve fitting was performed using Origin 2015. NMR cross-saturation experiments were performed with 222 μM 2H, 15N-labeled 14-3-3ζ in complex with 1.25 equivalent of dpFOXO3a, containing 20% 2H2O/80% 2H2O and selectively saturated dpFOXO3a by irradiating the aliphatic proton resonances, using the mlevsp180.p30 decoupling program. The saturation frequency was set at 1.0 ppm, and the saturation time was set to 1.0 s.

Competition analysis of 126 μM 2H, 15N-labeled dpFOXO3a with 1.1 equivalents of DNA and 1.5 equivalents of 14-3-3ζ dimer were monitored using 1H-15N TROSY spectrum at 600 and 800 MHz. The diluted sample (16 μM dpFOXO3a with 18 μM DNA plus 24 μM 14-3-3ζ) was also monitored using 1H-15N TROSY spectrum at 600 MHz. NMR samples were analyzed by gel filtration using SuperdexTM 200 increase 10/300 GL (Cytiva).

In the magnetic field- and temperature-dependent analyses, we prepared 209 μM 2H, 15N-labeled 14-3-3ζ with 1.25 equivalent of dpFOXO3a and measured 1H-15N TROSY spectra at 1 GHz at different temperatures: 303 K, 298 K, and 293 K.

## Your Original Review (Round 1)

### Reviewer 1

The manuscript "14-3-3ζ interacts with DNA binding domain of FOXO3a and competitively dissociates DNA by dual motif tethering" by Enomoto et al. studies the FOXO3a/14-3-3 ζ /DNA ternary system by ITC, FSEC and NMR. This is another example of a protein fully displacing DNA in spite of similar affinities. At first glance, this is counter-intuitive, but it adds to a growing number of systems where such behavior has been identified.

In principle I think the manuscript is scientifically sound and of broad interest to warrant publication in Nature Communications. However, I would request additional experiments and edits from the authors as follows:
1) Can the authors confirm their key finding (full displacement of DNA by an equimolar amount of 14-3-3 to dpFOXO3a) by a method different from FSEC? FSEC is not an equilibrium method, and on/off kinetics may play a role and confound the analysis. Could the authors demonstrate this key finding e.g. by NMR?
2) The affinity of 14-3-3 to FOXO3a is 2-fold higher than the affinity of DNA to FOXO3a, hence displacement of DNA by 14-3-3 is only quantitatively, but not qualitatively, surprising. The authors also have the monophosphorylated system pS253-FOXO3a (T32A) which binds much weaker to 14-3-3 but still partially displaces DNA. Could the authors please perform a titration and present the full competition analysis with pS253-FOXO3a (T32A), as they did for dpFOXO3a ?
3) Please define the term “competitiveness” briefly and verbally in the main text, without the equation used in the Supplemental Information
4) Please move Supplementary Table 2 to the main text, as it is important to understand the argument.
5) The Kd value of 5–30 μM for the FOXO3a –14-3-3ζ interaction is quite confusing. Which FOXO3a construct was used for this experiment? I assume it is only the DBD, but this is not clearly stated, and why does the paragraph then often refer to the protein as dpFOXO3a ?
6) The Figure numbering is off for several Figures
Points 1 and 2 will need additional experiments, but I feel only these additional experiments will make the paper really valuable for publication in Nature Communications.

### Reviewer 2

Foxo3a is a well-established tumor-suppressive transcription factor that activates the expression of various anti-proliferative and pro-apoptotic genes. The 14-3-3 protein binds to diphosphorylated Foxo3a at threonine 32 (T32) and serine 253 (S253), inhibiting its DNA-binding activity. However, the precise mechanism of this inhibition remains unclear.
This manuscript investigates the potential mechanism by which 14-3-3 binding displaces Foxo3a from DNA, despite the phosphorylation sites of Foxo3a being distant from the DNA-binding domain (DBD). Using a combination of biophysical approaches—FSEC, ITC, and NMR—the authors propose that 14-3-3 interacts not only with the phosphorylated sites but also directly with the DBD of Foxo3a. They further suggest a two-step mechanism: initial binding of 14-3-3 to site P1 of Foxo3a forms a ternary complex, followed by the binding of a second 14-3-3 molecule that facilitates dissociation of Foxo3a from DNA.
Major Points for Consideration:
1. Novelty of the Findings:
The novelty of the findings needs to be clearly demonstrated. A similar study was published in ACS Omega (Vol. 7, Issue 28, July 5, 2022), titled “Structure of a 14-3-3ε:FOXO3a-pS253 Phosphopeptide Complex Reveals 14-3-3 Isoform-Specific Binding of Forkhead Box Class O Transcription Factor (FOXO) Phosphoproteins.” That paper reported that 14-3-3ε binding induces conformational changes that reposition critical arginine residues in Foxo3a, reducing its DNA-binding affinity.
While the current manuscript presents NMR-based data identifying additional critical residues upon protein interaction, the novelty and functional significance of these residues in regulating Foxo3a's DNA-binding activity have not been fully validated. For instance, site-directed mutagenesis of 14-3-3 residues in contact with the Foxo3a DBD could provide direct evidence of their role in Foxo3a displacement. Crosslinking experiments using chemical or UV crosslinkers, followed by identification of the crosslinked amino acids, would also significantly strengthen the conclusions.
Additionally, the NMR data indicate several residues involved in direct contact between the proteins. However, it remains unclear to an NMR nonspecialist whether these residues reflect direct interactions or result from allosteric conformational changes. This distinction should be clarified.
The weak binding of DBD to 14-3-3ζ was indicated only by NMR chemical shift and affinity measurements (Page 8, The Kd value for the DBD – 14-3-3ζ interaction was calculated to be 5–30 μM). However, without high-resolution structural data (such as crystal structures or cryo-EM) it is hard to support the mechanistic conclusions of this manuscript. Furthermore, the dynamic exchange model was primarily based on NMR signal splitting phenomena (e.g., splitting of the E202 signal into A and B, Figure 9a), but it was not validated through blocking exchange with mutants or real-time kinetic experiments, nor supported by structural data. Moreover, the hypothesis that DBD rapidly exchanges between 14-3-3ζ dimers was not substantiated by resolving the complex structure with individual monomers or through direct functional experiments. These gaps may lead to conclusions that exceed the scope of data support.
2. Figure Mislabeling:
The manuscript contains mislabeled or missing figure numbers (e.g., no Figure 6), leading to confusion and hindering the review process. This oversight suggests a lack of thorough proofreading prior to submission and should be corrected to maintain clarity and professionalism.
Minor Points:
1. Kd Determination Using Truncated Protein:
The dissociation constant (Kd) was determined using a truncated version of Foxo3a (residues 1–284). It is important to address whether this truncated construct behaves similarly to the full-length protein in Kd values. Is there any evidence that the full-length and truncated forms have comparable Kd values?
2. Incorrect Literature Citation:
On page 5, line 96, the cited papers focus on Foxo4 rather than Foxo3a. Please ensure that the references are relevant and specific to the subject of the manuscript.
3. Limited Evidence for Direct DBD Interaction:
The proposed direct binding of 14-3-3 to the DBD of Foxo3a and the suggested hybrid binding model are currently supported solely by NMR data, which were obtained using the truncated protein and peptides. This weakens the overall conclusion. Crosslinking experiments and site-specific mutagenesis would provide more robust support for these claims.
4. Inadequate Comparison with Existing Studies:
The authors only mentioned the similar mechanism of FOXO4 but did not conduct a detailed comparison of the phosphorylation site specificity, DBD structural differences, or functional regulatory similarities and differences between FOXO3a and FOXO4, leading to limited innovation in this study. It is recommended to include a structural and functional comparison between FOXO3a and FOXO4 in the Discussion section and to discuss other subtypes of the 14-3-3 family.

Foxo3a is a well-established tumor-suppressive transcription factor that activates the expression
of various anti-proliferative and pro-apoptotic genes. The 14-3-3 protein binds to
diphosphorylated Foxo3a at threonine 32 (T32) and serine 253 (S253), inhibiting its DNA-binding
activity. However, the precise mechanism of this inhibition remains unclear.
This manuscript investigates the potential mechanism by which 14-3-3 binding displaces Foxo3a
from DNA, despite the phosphorylation sites of Foxo3a being distant from the DNA-binding
domain (DBD). Using a combination of biophysical approaches—FSEC, ITC, and NMR—the
authors propose that 14-3-3 interacts not only with the phosphorylated sites but also directly with
the DBD of Foxo3a. They further suggest a two-step mechanism: initial binding of 14-3-3 to site
P1 of Foxo3a forms a ternary complex, followed by the binding of a second 14-3-3 molecule that
facilitates dissociation of Foxo3a from DNA.
Thank you for your thorough review and clear summary of our manuscript. We appreciate your
valuable suggestions for additional experiments and edits. We agree with Reviewer #2’s comments
and have revised the manuscript accordingly, as detailed below.
1. Novelty of the Findings:
1-1. The novelty of the findings needs to be clearly demonstrated. A similar study was published in
ACS Omega (Vol. 7, Issue 28, July 5, 2022), titled “Structure of a 14-3-3ε:FOXO3a-pS253
Phosphopeptide Complex Reveals 14-3-3 Isoform-Specific Binding of Forkhead Box Class O
Transcription Factor (FOXO) Phosphoproteins.” That paper reported that 14-3-3ε binding
induces conformational changes that reposition critical arginine residues in Foxo3a, reducing its
DNA-binding affinity.
Thank you for your comment. The novelty of our study lies in demonstrating that 14-3-3ζ
inhibits the dpFOXO3a–DNA binding primarily through direct interaction with the DBD, rather than
solely via the phosphorylated P2 motif, and in revealing a two-step displacement mechanism. While
we are aware of the ACS Omega study reporting 14-3-3ε binding to the P2 phosphopeptide
( RRRAV-pS -MD ) and the resulting reduction in DNA-binding affinity, our work shows that,
248 253 255
in the dpFOXO3a–DNA interaction, the contribution of helix 3 in the DBD to DNA binding is
substantially greater than that of the P2 motif. This conclusion is supported by a previous Nucleic
Acids Research study (Vol. 35, No. 20, 2007) reporting a K of 295 nM (ΔG = 37 kJ mol⁻¹) for wild-
d
type FOXO3a (158–253) binding to DNA and 1178 nM (ΔG = 34 kJ mol⁻¹) for the
R248A/R249A/R250A mutant. The ΔG difference of 3 kJ mol⁻¹ corresponds to only ~8% of the total
binding free energy, indicating that residues R248–R250 make a minor contribution compared to the
DBD.
Importantly, our NMR competition experiments demonstrated that a ternary dpFOXO3a–DNA–
14-3-3ζ complex can form, indicating that binding of 14-3-3ζ to the P2 site alone does not induce
DNA dissociation (Supplementary Fig. 5 and 6). This finding argues against a P2-centric model (as
suggested in ACS Omega, 2022) and supports our conclusion that DNA displacement requires the
additional engagement of 14-3-3ζ with the DBD.
Therefore, inhibition via the 14-3-3ζ–DBD interaction is expected to be more effective than
through the 14-3-3ζ–P2 interaction. We have revised the manuscript to clarify this point in the

and (ii) revealing a two-step displacement mechanism. Although the P2 also interacts with the DNA
(Nucleic Acids Research, Vol. 35, No. 20, 2007) and behaves as the competitive site for DNA and

Thank you for this important suggestion. On the 14-3-3ζ side, CSP mapping was already
presented in the original manuscript; however, because CSP can reflect not only direct
intermolecular contacts but also conformational changes upon binding, in this revision we applied
NMR cross-saturation experiments, which selectively detect residues in close spatial proximity (~5
Å) to dpFOXO3a, making them particularly suitable for directly identifying the interaction surface.
Among the residues identified on 14-3-3ζ, several were located away from the canonical phospho-
motif binding groove and positioned such that they are likely to interact with the DBD of FOXO3a.
From these, we selected two residue clusters (D197/E198/E202/D204 and
T215/L216/Q219/R222) as representative contact sites for mutagenesis. We generated quadruple-
alanine mutants targeting these residues and tested them in FSEC-based competition assays;
although the mutants did not show a major reduction in DNA displacement ability (Supplementary
Fig. 13), this outcome is likely due to the broad protein–protein interaction surface, where disruption
of only part of the interface is insufficient to abolish binding.
In contrast, NMR spectral changes of [2H, 15N]-CTD titrated with the
T215A/L216A/Q219A/R222A mutant of 14-3-3ζ revealed that signals mainly in helix 3 shifted in
different direction or decreased in intensity compared with titration using wildtype 14-3-3ζ.
This supports a direct contribution of these residues to the DBD – 14-3-3ζ interface. In the case of the
D197A/E198A/E202A/D204A mutant, precipitation prevented collection of sufficient NMR data.
These NMR observations therefore strongly suggest that the helix 3 of the DBD directly interacts
with residues around T215/L216/Q219/R222 of 14-3-3ζ (Supplementary Fig. 14).
For completeness, we note that on the FOXO3a side, CSP analysis identified residues around
helix 3 of the DBD as part of the interface; however, because this region overlaps with the DBD–
DNA binding site, mutagenesis was not feasible without perturbing DNA binding directly.
Taken together, these results provide direct experimental evidence for the physical interaction
between dpFOXO3a and 14-3-3ζ, and clarify why even multiple-site mutations on 14-3-3ζ were
insufficient to eliminate the interaction. We have clarified these points in the Results sections (page
11, lines 240–255) and added new figures highlighting the identified residues on both proteins, as
follows:

(residues 1–284) behaves similarly to the full-length protein in binding affinity measurements. Based
on previous studies, the DNA-binding activity of full-length FOXO3a is dominated by the DBD
(Cell Death Dis. 14, 702, 2023). While the transactivation domain (TAD) can interact with the DBD
and compete with DNA (J. Mol. Biol. 384, 3, 2008; ACS Chem. Biol. 4, 12, 2009), the DNA–DBD
interaction is strong enough to displace the TAD (ACS Chem. Biol. 4, 12, 2009), suggesting minimal
influence on DNA binding.

DBD and 14-3-3ζ. While the TAD of the full-length protein could, in principle, compete with 14-3-
3ζ for the DBD, its competitiveness is expected to be lower than that of 14-3-3ζ, as it is also lower

domain (TAD) can compete with DNA for the DBD (J. Mol. Biol. 384, 3, 2008; ACS Chem. Biol. 4,
12, 2009), the DNA–DBD interaction is strong enough to displace the TAD (ACS Chem. Biol. 4, 12,
2009). For 14-3-3ζ binding, the recognition of the two phosphorylated motifs (P1 and P2) of
FOXO3a is known to be dominant.”

cancers (Expert Opin. Ther. Targets, 14, 12, 2010), these findings may have broad implications for
therapeutic strategies targeting FOXO–14-3-3 complexes, particularly in disease contexts, especially

## Paper

## Abstract

In cancer cells, Ras protein mutations activate a signaling cascade that phosphorylates kinases, transcription, and translation factors, driving cancer cell proliferation. One such factor, FOXO3a, promotes apoptosis-related gene transcription. However, in many cancer cells, FOXO3a is phosphorylated and is bound to 14-3-3ζ at phosphorylation sites. The 14-3-3ζ binding displaces phosphorylated FOXO3a from DNA, suppressing apoptosis. Since the phosphorylation sites are far from the DNA-binding domain (DBD) of FOXO3a, the mechanism of displacement remains unclear. Using isothermal titration calorimetry and fluorescence-detection size-exclusion chromatography, we find that 14-3-3ζ strongly displaces DNA from di-phosphorylated FOXO3a (dpFOXO3a), despite similar dissociation constants for dpFOXO3a–14-3-3ζ and dpFOXO3a–DNA. Nuclear magnetic resonance data identify weak, but direct binding of 14-3-3ζ to the DBD, suggesting direct competition. These findings suggest that 14-3-3ζ enhances its competitive ability by dual tethering to the DBD of FOXO3a via phosphorylation sites, effectively displacing DNA.

## Introduction

In cancer cells, Ras proteins are activated by mutations independently of upstream regulators, initiating a signaling cascade. This cascade consists of the sequential phosphorylation of three or more kinases, ultimately leading to the phosphorylation of effector proteins involved in transcription and translation1. Phosphorylation up- or down-regulates effector protein function, causing uncontrolled cell proliferation, apoptosis evasion, invasion, and metastasis1. One such effector protein is FOXO3a, which is a transcriptional activator of genes encoding a number of apoptosis-related proteins such as Bim and FasL that inhibit the cell proliferation2–4. However, in tumor cells transcriptional activity of FOXO3a is inhibited upon its phosphorylation and subsequent binding of an adaptor protein, 14-3-3ζ, resulting in cancer progression via cancer cell apoptosis suppression2.

FOXO3a (a 71 kDa protein consisting of 673 residues) is a member of the forkhead box (FOX) protein family. FOXO3a comprises a DNA-binding domain (DBD), also called the forkhead domain (residues 157–250), and intrinsically disordered regions in the N- and C-terminals (Fig. 1)5,6. The DBD binds to specific DNA sequences (referred to as FOXO-responsive elements, FREs), triggering apoptosis-related gene transcription. In tumor cells, FOXO3a is phosphorylated at three residues (T32, S253, and S315) in the intrinsically disordered regions by an upstream kinase, AKT. Subsequently, its transcriptional activity is inhibited by the binding of an adaptor protein, 14-3-3ζ2, which is highly expressed in cancer cells7.

14-3-3ζ, a member of the 14-3-3 protein family, is a 245-residue acidic protein, consisting of nine α-helices. 14-3-3ζ exists and functions as an axisymmetric dimer8. 14-3-3ζ binds to the Ser/Thr-phosphorylated motifs in its target proteins and prevents their dephosphorylation, prolonging the functional regulation by phosphorylation9. 14-3-3ζ recognizes two phosphorylated motifs in the N-terminal region of FOXO3a (P1: RPRSC-pT-WPLQR, P2: RRRAV-pS-MDNSN)2,10,11. Upon binding to the phosphorylated FOXO3a, 14-3-3ζ dissociates FOXO3a from FREs, thereby inhibiting its transcriptional activity2,12,13. Furthermore, 14-3-3ζ masks the nuclear localization signal (RRR) of FOXO3a located within the P2 site, facilitating the export of FOXO3a from the nucleus to the cytoplasm14,15. In the cytoplasm, FOXO3a is ubiquitinated and subject to degradation16,17. Consequently, FOXO3a-mediated apoptosis is suppressed, leading to malignant cancer transformation. Reportedly, cancer cell apoptosis is enhanced by inhibiting the interaction between phosphorylated FOXO3a and 14-3-3ζ18. Therefore, inhibiting the interaction is a viable target for anticancer drugs. Although understanding the mechanism of action is important, it remains unknown how the 14-3-3ζ binding dissociates FOXO3a from its target DNA sequence, as the 14-3-3ζ binding sites, P1 and P2, located remotely from the DBD.

This dissociation mechanism has been mainly studied using FOXO4, which has a similar structure to a member of the FOXO family19. FOXO4 has high sequence identity with FOXO3a at P1 (100%), P2 (86%), and the DBD (83%), supporting the assumption that their interaction modes with DNA and 14-3-3ζ are highly similar, and thus that Kd values of FOXO4 provide a reliable reference for FOXO3a. A previous study12 showed that 14-3-3ζ dissociates di-phosphorylated FOXO4 (dpFOXO4) from the DNA with the human insulin response element (hIRE). This result was attributed to the difference in dissociation constants (Kds), which were reported to be 30 nM for dpFOXO4–14-3-3ζ and 500 nM for dpFOXO4–hIRE. However, as the consensus DNA sequence recognized by the FOXO family (e.g., daf-16 binding element, DBE)20 has higher affinity for FOXO3a than for hIRE21, the relative binding affinity of phosphorylated FOXO3a for DBE and 14-3-3ζ should be analyzed quantitatively under the same conditions to conclude that the dissociation is caused by the difference in their Kd values.

In another study, the binding mode of the DBD of FOXO4 and the 14-3-3ζ dimer was deduced based on the distance constraints obtained from fluorescence resonance energy transfer (FRET) experiments using 14-3-3ζ ‘monomeric mutants’ and a FOXO4 fragment, which contained the DBD and was mono-phosphorylated at the P2 site22. However, the direct interaction between the 14-3-3ζ dimer and the DBD within dpFOXO4 has not yet been experimentally observed.

Here, we quantitatively analyze the binding affinity and competition of di-phosphorylated FOXO3a (dpFOXO3a), DNA, and 14-3-3ζ using isothermal titration calorimetry (ITC) and fluorescence-detection size-exclusion chromatography (FSEC). In addition, we execute NMR analyses on the interaction between dpFOXO3a and 14-3-3ζ. Based on these results, we propose a mechanism of the FOXO3a dissociation from DNA by the 14-3-3ζ binding.
